'''Carolyn Cohen''' (June 18, 1929 – December 20, 2017)<ref name=NAS>{{cite web|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/carolyn-cohen-743boy/|title=Carolyn Cohen|publisher=National Academy of Sciences|access-date=December 24, 2017}}</ref> was an American biologist and biophysicist. She was a Fellow of the [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]].

==Early life and education==
Carolyn Cohen was born June 18, 1929, to parents Anna and Philip Cohen.<ref name=NAS/><ref name=Globe>{{cite news|title=Carolyn Cohen Obituary |newspaper=The Boston Globe |date=8 January 2018 |url=https://www.legacy.com/us/obituaries/bostonglobe/name/carolyn-cohen-obituary?id=1618281 |accessdate=4 January 2023}}</ref> After Cohen's father died in 1939, she credited his lawyer Samuel Sumner Goldberg for mentoring her and nurturing her curiosity.<ref name=Globe/><ref name="Mrs. Professor"/> Cohen attended Joan of Arc Junior High School, then the selective [[Hunter College High School]].<ref name="Mrs. Professor">{{cite journal|last=Cohen|first=Carolyn|title=Mrs. Professor|journal=The Journal of Biological Chemistry|date=September 16, 2011|volume=286|issue=37|pages=31929–31931|doi=10.1074/jbc.X111.287250|doi-access=free |pmid=21799004|pmc=3173190}}</ref> After rejections from [[McGill University]] and [[Barnard College]], Cohen's French teacher urged her to apply to [[Bryn Mawr College]], where she was accepted with a full-tuition scholarship.<ref name="Mrs. Professor"/> In the summer of 1949, Cohen took a job in the kitchen of the [[Marine Biological Laboratory]] at [[Woods Hole, MA]].<ref name=Memoir1/> There she met [[Shinya Inoué]], worked for [[Otto Schmitt]], and attended a lecture by [[Dorothy Wrinch]] that she later credited with stimulating her career interest in [[protein structure]]s.<ref name=Memoir1/> Cohen completed her Bachelor of Arts in Biology and Physics from Bryn Mawr in 1950, graduating summa cum laude.<ref>{{Cite web|url=http://www.brandeis.edu/facultyguide/person.html?emplid=10c26496511e9dcc5ae2cab67dacf8c0a29e75ec|title=Carolyn Cohen &#124; Brandeis University |website=www.brandeis.edu|language=en|accessdate=February 7, 2017}}</ref> She then moved to [[Massachusetts Institute of Technology]], for a PhD under the supervision of Richard S. Bear. There she worked on the structure of [[collagen]] and other helically structured proteins, completing her degree in 1954.<ref name=Memoir1>{{Cite journal|last=Cohen|first=Carolyn|date=2007-11-09|title=Seeing and Knowing in Structural Biology|journal=Journal of Biological Chemistry|volume=282|issue=45|pages=32529–32538|doi=10.1074/jbc.X700001200|issn=0021-9258|pmid=17848543|doi-access=free}}</ref>

While at MIT, Cohen met then-visiting researcher [[Jean Hanson]], who was  working on the structure of muscle fibers. After graduation Cohen took a [[postdoctoral researcher]] position in Hanson's laboratory at [[King's College London]], working on the [[X-ray crystallography]] structure of [[actin]] filaments.<ref name=Memoir1/> After nine months, Cohen returned to MIT working first in Bear's lab, then with [[Andrew Szent-Györgyi]] on the structure of fibrous proteins. She enrolled in medical school at [[Boston University]], but left after less than a month, returning to full-time research at MIT.<ref name=Memoir1/> In 1957, she began what would become a long collaboration with [[Donald Caspar]], investigating the structure of [[tropomyosin]].<ref name=Memoir1/>

==Academic career==
In 1958, Cohen started her own laboratory, co-led by Caspar, at the Children's Cancer Research Foundation (now the [[Dana–Farber Cancer Institute]]).<ref name=Memoir1/> There she worked primarily on the structure of myosin. With postdoctoral fellow [[Susan Lowey]], Cohen predicted a model for the myosin structure with an [[alpha-helix|alpha-helical]] core bookended by globular masses. Studying the catch muscle in [[Mytilus edulis|molluscs]], Cohen and [[Kenneth Holmes]] (then a postdoctoral researcher with Caspar) demonstrated the presence of alpha-helical [[coiled coil]] filaments, published in 1963.<ref name=Memoir1/> A few years later in 1967, Lowey and [[Henry S. Slater]] confirmed the predicted globular heads by [[electron microscopy]].<ref name=Memoir1/> From 1969 to 1972, Cohen and Caspar published a series of papers describing the structure of tropomyosin – the first protein structure determined by electron microscopy.<ref name=Memoir1/>

In 1972, Cohen, Caspar, and Lowe – together called the "Structural Biology Laboratory" – moved their laboratory to become the first research group at [[Brandeis University]]'s Rosenstiel Basic Medical Sciences Research Center.<ref name=Memoir1/> In fact, Cohen was the first tenured woman in Biology at Brandeis University.<ref>{{Cite web |title=Office of the Vice Provost for Research |url=https://www.brandeis.edu/research/administration/index.html |access-date=2025-02-27 |website=www.brandeis.edu |language=en}}</ref>

Cohen retired from Brandeis in 2012.<ref>{{cite web|title=Retiring faculty members honored at luncheon|url=http://www.brandeis.edu/now/2012/may/retirees.html|accessdate=October 25, 2012}}</ref>

In honor of her work surrounding protein structures, in 2022 the Biophysical Society Innovation Award was renamed to the Carolyn Cohen Award for Biophysical Innovation. It has since been presented every year at the BPS Annual Meeting in February.<ref>{{Cite web |title=BPS Innovation Award Renamed in Honor of Carolyn Cohen |url=https://www.biophysics.org/bps-bulletin/bps-innovation-award-renamed-in-honor-of-carolyn-cohen |access-date=2025-02-01 |website=The Biophysical Society |language=en-US}}</ref>

==Awards and honors==
* Fellow, [[American Academy of Arts and Sciences]]
* Member, [[National Academy of Sciences]]
* 2000, Biophysical Society Founder's Award for her accomplishments in [[Biophysics]]{{citation needed|date=December 2017}}
